newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU revises air liability rules for bloc carriers.
newsitem.headline: EU revises air liability rules for bloc carriers.

text.p: European Union officials corrected on Friday details they gave on Thursday about the bloc's planned fast-track system obliging airlines to pay compensation to passengers or their relatives after a crash.

Officials released a series of figures during Thursday's Transport Council which spoke of payouts in European currency units when they should have referred to "special drawing rights" (SDR), a currency basket with specific weightings of major traded currencies.
The error deflated the value of payouts required of airlines in the event of a crash by a factor of about 1.2, officials said on Friday.

Ministers agreed on Thursday that airlines should make a minimum, non-refundable payout of 15,000 SDR ($23,000) to victims or their dependents in the immediate aftermath of a crash, down from 50,000 SDR ($75,000) proposed by the European Commission.

The new rules would make airlines strictly liable for 100,000 SDR ($150,000) per person in the event of a crash, meaning they could not exclude or limit their liability for that sum by proving no fault.
Ministers also agreed that new liability rules would apply to all EU carriers but not to those of third countries operating to and from airports in the 15-country bloc.
Third-country operators would have the option of complying with the rules or stating clearly their non-compliance in travellers' documents, one EU official told Reuters on Friday.
Final adoption of the rules, which would signal their immediate entry into force, now depends on Euro-MPs' agreement.

The proposal would protect passengers from terrorist attacks where there is currently no cover. Carriers would be required to pay out the 15,000 SDR compensation within 15 days of a passenger's death or up to a ceiling of 15,000 SDR in the event of injury.
The Commission had proposed a 10-day maximum pay-out delay.

Ministers also rejected a Commission proposal that crash victims or their dependents be able to pursue court action in their home courts rather than in the carrier's country of origin, its main place of business or at the beginning or end of the ticketed journey.
The proposal would abolish the current $10,000 ceiling on liability per passenger in the event of injury or death in a crash and extend the liability cover to domestic flights in the 15-country bloc.
Existing rules, as defined under 1929 Warsaw Convention and other agreements, currently apply only to international flights.
